You'd never expect rocks to move by themselves.
But in Death Valley, they leave tracks up to 100 meters long. What moves them, actually?
That's the first of six strange places on Earth.
For each one, we'll look at what scientists actually found, and give an honest verdict: solved, best guess, or still unknown.
Number one: the sailing stones.
In Death Valley National Park in California, there's a dry lake bed called Racetrack Playa. It's flat, cracked, and almost perfectly level.
Scattered across it are rocks. And behind many of them are long, shallow trails, as if the rocks had slid across the ground on their own.
Some trails are straight. Some curve. Some rocks that start side by side travel together for a while, and then one turns away.
The first written account comes from 1915, when a prospector named Joseph Crook visited the playa.
For almost a century after that, nobody saw a rock move. People blamed strong winds, dust devils, and slippery mud.
Then, in the winter of 2013 and 2014, a research team put GPS trackers inside some rocks and set up time-lapse cameras around the playa.
And they got lucky. On the twentieth of December, 2013, they watched more than sixty rocks move at once.
Here's what happens. Rain or snowmelt makes a shallow pond on the playa. On cold winter nights, the water freezes into a sheet of ice just a few millimeters thick.
On a sunny morning, the ice starts to break into large thin panels. Light winds push the panels across the water, and the panels shove the rocks along the soft mud underneath.
The rocks move slowly, up to about five meters a minute. Some moves lasted up to sixteen minutes, and some rocks moved more than two hundred meters that winter.
It only happens when the playa floods and then freezes, so in many winters, nothing moves at all.
Verdict: solved. Thin sheets of ice, pushed by wind.
Number two: the eye of the Sahara.
In the desert of Mauritania, in West Africa, there's a giant bull's-eye. It's called the Richat Structure, or the Eye of Africa.
It's about 40 kilometers across. From the ground, it's hard to even notice. But from space, it's unmistakable.
NASA says it became a landmark for space shuttle crews.
Because it's so round, scientists first thought a meteorite had made it.
But when they studied the rocks in the 1950s and 60s, they found none of the signs a high-speed impact leaves behind.
The real story is slower. Long ago, molten rock pushed up from below and bent the layers above it into a dome.
Over a very long time, wind and water wore the top of that dome away. The harder rock layers survived as rings, and the softer ones eroded into valleys between them.
That's why the oldest rocks are in the center, and the rings get younger as you move outward.
The area is also full of ancient stone tools, left by early humans long before the desert was what it is today.
Online, some people claim it's the lost city of Atlantis, because Plato described Atlantis as a city of rings.
But there's no archaeological evidence of a city there, and no sign of the canals Plato described. Most scholars think Atlantis was a story Plato invented.
Verdict: solved. An eroded rock dome, not a crater, and not Atlantis.
Number three: the pink lake.
On Middle Island, off the south coast of Western Australia, there's a lake that's bright pink.
It's called Lake Hillier. It's about 600 meters long, and only a thin strip of sand and forest separates it from the dark blue ocean.
The pink doesn't come from the light. If you scoop the water into a bottle, it stays pink.
The explorer Matthew Flinders wrote about the lake in 1802.
So where does the color come from? Life.
The water is extremely salty. And very few things can live in it. One that can is a tiny alga called Dunaliella salina. Scientists believe it's the main source of the pink.
A genetic study of the lake also found salt-loving bacteria, like Salinibacter ruber, and other microbes.
In recent years, heavy rain has diluted the lake and faded its color. Scientists expect the pink to come back as the water level drops.
Verdict: solved. Salt-loving microbes paint the lake pink.
Number four: the door to hell.
In the middle of the Karakum Desert in Turkmenistan, there's a crater that has been on fire for decades.
It's about 60 to 70 meters wide and 30 meters deep. Hundreds of natural gas fires burn across its floor and rim.
It's called the Darvaza gas crater, or simply the door to hell. It became the country's top tourist attraction.
The most common story goes like this. In 1971, Soviet engineers were drilling for oil and gas. The drill hit a cavern of natural gas, and the ground collapsed.
To stop poisonous gas from spreading, they set it on fire, expecting it to burn out in a few days. It didn't.
But here's the problem. The records from that time are missing, classified, or out of reach.
Some local geologists say the crater actually formed in the 1960s, and was only set on fire in the 1980s.
In 2022, Turkmenistan's president announced plans to put the fire out. By 2025, officials said the fire had shrunk to a third of its size, after new wells were drilled around it to capture the gas.
Verdict: best guess. Drilling and a gas fire, but nobody is sure exactly when or how it started.
Number five: the fairy circles.
In the Namib Desert in southern Africa, the grass is covered in bare, round patches, each surrounded by a ring of taller grass.
They appear across a band of desert about 2,400 kilometers long. They're called fairy circles.
In 2014, similar circles were also found in the Pilbara region of Western Australia.
Scientists have argued about them for decades, and there are two main camps.

The first camp blames termites. In 2013, a researcher named Norbert Juergens found sand termites in almost every circle he studied. The idea is that they eat the grass roots, and the bare patch traps rainwater underground.
The second camp says the grass does it to itself. In a very dry place, plants compete for water, and that competition can naturally space them out into a regular pattern.
In 2022, one team dug up hundreds of grasses inside and around the circles. They found the grass had died from lack of water, not from termites eating the roots.
And in Australia, the Aboriginal Martu people have long linked the circles to harvester termites, and a 2023 study with them supported that idea there.
Verdict: still unknown. Termites, thirsty grass, or maybe both.
Number six: the lights of Hessdalen.
In a quiet valley in central Norway, people have reported strange lights since at least the 1930s.
The Hessdalen lights are usually white, yellow, or red. They can float slowly, hover in the air, or race across the valley. Some last a few seconds. Some last more than an hour.
Between late 1981 and mid-1984, they were seen fifteen to twenty times a week, and tourists came to watch.
In 1983, volunteers started Project Hessdalen to study them. And in 1998, an automatic measuring station was set up in the valley to record the lights.
Some sightings turned out to be stars, planes, car headlights, or mirages. But not all of them.

There are several ideas. One says dust from the area's rocks burns in the air in an unusual way. Another says radioactive radon gas from the ground could turn dusty air into glowing plasma. Another points to electric charges from quartz in the rocks.
None of these has been proven.
Verdict: still unknown. The lights are real. What makes them isn't clear.
So, let's check the scoreboard.
The sailing stones: solved. Ice and wind.
The eye of the Sahara: solved. An eroded dome.
The pink lake: solved. Salt-loving microbes.
The door to hell: best guess. A drilling accident and a gas fire.
The fairy circles: still unknown.
The Hessdalen lights: still unknown.
Three solved, one best guess, and two we still can't explain. Our own planet still has places that keep scientists guessing.
